Notably, a network having both 3- and 5-fold defects with a total defect fraction of 7.4% reverses the typical boron-dominant response of other cases, becoming more sensitive to phosphorus. Tauc and optical sum-rule analyses further indicate that network topology defines the broader optical landscape, whereas doping primarily affects states near the gap and redistributes spectral weight. These findings establish defect topology as a microscopic control parameter that links amorphous structure, dopant activity, and optical response in amorphous silicon.

items.title: Cumulant dynamics of the ferromagnetic dipolar XY model
authors: Jinxin Yang, Alberto R. Cavallar, Lode Pollet
items.summary: We study the second-order truncated cumulant dynamics for the preparation of dynamical states in the dipolar ferromagnetic XY model on the square lattice for system sizes up to linear size L = 60. The observations lead to a transparent picture in which a coherent region of finite extent and finite magnetization forms, which is possible even for diabatic but sufficiently slow ramps. These two scales are functions of the ramp constant, the initial entropy of the system, and time. Our findings put strong requirements on future experiments addressing dipolar XY equilibrium physics in bigger system sizes.

items.title: Symmetry-Enabled Ferroelectric Valley Transduction in Rhombohedral Bilayer WSe$_2$
authors: Katsunori Wakabayashi, Souren Adhikary, Tomoaki Kameda, Kazuhito Tsukagoshi
items.summary: Ferroelectric polarization couples to the layer degree of freedom in a bilayer, but a valley-selective energy response requires the valleys to carry different interlayer character. Rhombohedral bilayer WSe$_2$ meets that condition by symmetry: three-fold rotation forbids interlayer tunneling at the $K$ valley, while strong hybridization remains at $\Gamma$. The resulting contrast converts the band-effective ferroelectric layer asymmetry into a shift of the $K$ edge, and so displaces the $K$--$\Gamma$ landscape: a finite-field fit that does not impose the rule leaves the $K$ coupling consistent with zero, and the shift reaches \polshiftdft~meV, the most that asymmetry can give a single valley. Reversing the polarization mirrors the valley landscape in displacement field, so the two registries have equal and opposite differential transconductance $g_d$ at zero field. In the ideal symmetric limit a second parity holds about each registry's own compensation field and places a zero of $g_d$ there. The valley-dependent screening calculated here displaces that zero by only \gdnulllow\% at the read point, so device asymmetry limits the accuracy. The result links a known stacking selection rule to ferroelectric valley transduction, with a quantitative valley shift and a directly testable transport signature.

items.title: Engineering many-body tunneling dynamics of one-dimensional bosons with finite-core power-law interactions
authors: Abhik Kumar Saha, Cesare Vianello, Andrea Trombettoni, Barnali Chakrabarti
items.summary: We investigate the many-body dynamics of a one-dimensional Bose-Josephson junction of ultracold bosons in a box-like potential with a central barrier, interacting via finite-core power-law interactions $V_\alpha(r)=g/(r^\alpha+d^\alpha)$, where $d$ sets the short-distance scale and $\alpha$ controls the spatial dependence. Using the multiconfigurational time-dependent Hartree method for bosons (MCTDHB), we explore how the interaction profile and strength, barrier, and initial population imbalance shape tunneling dynamics. At weak interaction, increasing $\alpha$ drives a crossover from Josephson oscillations to dephasing and recurrent rephasing, demonstrating the importance of the interaction kernel's spatial structure. A higher barrier suppresses recurrences, whereas a larger initial imbalance promotes relaxation toward nearly vanishing population imbalance. Increasing interaction strength progressively suppresses population-transfer fluctuations, particularly at larger $\alpha$. The two-mode extended Bose-Hubbard model captures the dynamics when the lowest orbital in each well dominates, but loses accuracy as additional orbitals become populated. In the strongly interacting regime, many-body spatial structures develop and several natural orbitals are needed for converged dynamics, placing the system beyond a two-mode description. Our results establish the interaction profile and strength, barrier, and initial state as distinct control parameters for coherent, dephasing, recurrent, and suppressed many-body tunneling of one-dimensional bosons. The ability to tailor soft-core interactions via Rydberg dressing offers a promising route to exploring interaction-engineered tunneling in ultracold atoms.

items.title: Probe Dynamics in Active Baths via Trajectory-Response Relations
authors: Chul-Ung Woo, Jiwon Choi, Heiko Rieger
items.summary: Passive probes in active baths can undergo spontaneous motion driven by nonequilibrium forces that depend on probe velocity and interaction geometry. Using trajectory-response relations that express the bath response to a probe in terms of free-particle displacement statistics, we investigate the dynamics of freely moving probes weakly coupled to ideal active baths. The mean force exerted by the bath defines a velocity-space potential whose minima describe the stable states. By analyzing how the mean force depends on the probe velocity, we identify stable resting and moving states and determine the parameter regime in which they coexist. For elliptical interactions, the resting state becomes unstable first along the narrow axis, resulting in direction selection already at the linear-response level. For fourfold interactions, linear friction remains isotropic, while the nonlinear dependence of the mean force on probe velocity selects axial or diagonal motion and produces directional multistability. We further show that the trajectory-response relations extend to higher orders in the probe strength, where multi-interval free-particle trajectory statistics become relevant. For a Gaussian probe, these higher-order terms shift the speed of the stable moving state.

items.title: Competing lattice instabilities in epitaxially strained BaSnO3
items.summary: We use density functional theory to map the lattice-dynamical landscape of BaSnO3 under biaxial compressive strain and uncover the hierarchy of structural instabilities. Our results demonstrate that the phase stability of strained BaSnO3 cannot be inferred from the softening of the polar mode alone. Instead it is governed by the competition among lattice instabilities and their anharmonic coupling to structural relaxation. Two-mode energy-surface analyses show that the polar and rotational order parameters interact predominantly competitively. While A- and M-point octahedral rotations become unstable before the zone-center polar mode and dominate the harmonic response for moderate values of strain, they are related to a continuous transition without anharmonic lattice coupling and a moderate gain of energy with strain. Large strain may induce a first order transition to a supertetragonal polar state. Once this state is stabilized, the magnitude of polarization and ferroelectric energy well depth are comparable to BaTiO3 under compressive strain. Furthermore, we discuss how an electric field or electron doping may tip the balance between the different modes and favor of the supertetragonal structure over antipolar and rotational alternatives at a reduced critical strain.

items.title: Filling and Sealing Carbon Nanotubes by Local Anodic Oxidation
authors: Ruiqing Zang, Jianan Xiao, Jacob Bair, Ian Wang, Chuyue Peng, Matthias Kuehne
items.summary: Carbon nanotubes (CNTs) are prime nanofluidic conduits and nanopores for studying matter under extreme confinement. Since most synthesis routes yield CNTs with closed ends, opening and filling strategies are required to access their interior for fluid and ion transport, whereas studies of the encapsulated species themselves may additionally require sealing to prevent their escape in dry or vacuum environments. Capacitively coupled local anodic oxidation (LAO) in an atomic force microscope (AFM) has been shown to cut individual CNTs at predefined positions, but whether cutting induces opening, filling, or sealing has remained unclear. Using spatially resolved micro-Raman spectroscopy, we find that LAO cutting surprisingly produces filled CNT segments that remain sealed under dry Ar atmosphere for weeks. The magnitudes of the blueshift and broadening of the innermost-wall radial breathing-like mode are consistent with water filling, pointing to the water meniscus condensed between the AFM tip and the substrate as the source of CNT filling during cutting. High-vacuum annealing at 140 {\deg}C releases the encapsulated species from some, but not all, segments, indicating a thermally surmountable barrier rather than re-formed end caps. This one-step cut-fill-seal capability offers a route to diameter-resolved studies of nanoconfined water and aqueous solutions, and to zeptoliter-scale sample delivery for vacuum-based analytical techniques.

items.title: Single Spin Hall Conversion in the Hall Response of Magnetic-Insulator/Heavy-Metal Bilayers Identified by Odd Spin-Hall-Angle Dependence
authors: Akashdeep Akashdeep, Ewiese Mohammad Ababneh, Botros Gerges Mikhail Fenhas, Duc Minh Tran, Mathias Kl\"aui, Steven S. -L. Zhang, Vivek Amin, Gerhard Jakob, Timo Kuschel
items.summary: The Hall response of magnetic-insulator/heavy-metal bilayers is usually ascribed to two successive spin Hall conversions and is therefore expected to be even in the spin Hall angle. Using distinct magnetic-field windows, we separate the Hall voltage of yttrium iron garnet bilayers with Ta and Pt of opposite spin Hall angle into contributions from magnetization- and magnetic-field-driven precession as well as from ordinary Hall effect. The field-driven component reverses sign between Ta and Pt, revealing a Hall response odd-in-spin-Hall-angle. The magnetization-driven component also has opposite signs for Ta and Pt, except for the thinnest heavy-metal layers. A drift-diffusion model with interface-generated spin currents describes this behavior: the field-driven component is predominantly carried by a single spin Hall conversion, and the magnetization-driven component is consistent with one as well. Other potential explanations, based on a description with a finite imaginary spin-mixing conductance rather than interface-generated spin currents, require unusually large values of this conductance, making this mechanism unlikely. Our findings advance the understanding of Hall responses in magnetic-insulator/heavy-metal bilayers toward a more general description.

items.title: Machine-accelerated extraction of experimental superconducting parameters for physical insight and prediction across thousands of materials
authors: Mihir Manium, Benjamin Geisler, Peter J. Hirschfeld, Amalia I. Coldea
items.summary: New superconductors could unlock next-generation technologies from nuclear fusion to lossless electronics. Machine learning can predict candidate superconductors but lacks validated experimental training data beyond the critical temperature. Here we present AutoSuperCon, a database of eight superconducting parameters, containing 20354 entries for 6793 superconductors. The data were extracted from over 47000 arXiv preprints using a large language model and validated against reference datasets ($R^2 = 0.96$ with NIMS SuperCon). Using AutoSuperCon, we show that median gap ratios rise from 3.6 in conventional superconductors to 6.4 in cuprates, 28% of upper critical fields exceed the Pauli limit, and critical temperatures lie below a ceiling proportional to the superfluid density. Further, we train composition-based predictors for the critical temperature ($R^2_{\log}=0.83$) and the upper critical field ($R^2_{\log}=0.69$), boosted by transfer learning. Within known superconducting families, composition alone is sufficient to screen candidates for both parameters. AutoSuperCon thus enables physical insight and data-driven discovery across thousands of superconductors.

items.title: Cation-intermixing driven evolution from a narrow avoided crossing to an enlarged inverted gap in Ge$_2$Bi$_2$Te$_5$
authors: Alexander S. Frolov, Alexander V. Fedorov, Nadezhda V. Vladimirova, Sergey M. Aksenov, Mark A. Naumov, Savely V. Domenko, Artem A. Minaev, Vasily S. Stolyarov, Denis V. Vyalikh, Lada V. Yashina
items.summary: Combining the building blocks and structural motifs of the topological insulator Bi$_2$Te$_3$ and the ferroelectric Rashba semiconductor GeTe, we synthesized and comprehensively characterized the resulting Ge$_2$Bi$_2$Te$_5$ compound, which exhibits pronounced cation intermixing. Using momentum-resolved photoemission spectroscopy and ab initio calculations, we demonstrate how cation intermixing drives the evolution of its electronic structure from a narrow avoided crossing to a substantially enlarged inverted band gap. We establish the microscopic origin of this behavior in the redistribution of Ge and Bi atoms within the cation sublattice, which increases the contribution of Bi-derived states near the valence-band maximum and enhances the effective contribution of spin-orbit coupling, thereby stabilizing the topological electronic structure. Our findings demonstrate that cation disorder, which can be controlled during crystal growth, provides an additional degree of freedom for engineering topological electronic structures, opening new opportunities for the development of functional quantum materials.

items.title: Brute-force molecular dynamics simulation of aging in amorphous Ge$_2$Sb$_2$Te$_5$
authors: Elisa Petroni, Dario Baratella, Omar Abou El Kheir, Andrea Redaelli, Marco Bernasconi
items.summary: Chalcogenide alloys such as the prototypical Ge$_2$Sb$_2$Te$_5$ compound are used in phase change electronic memories due to their ability to undergo a fast and reversible transition between the amorphous and crystalline phases upon heating. The amorphous phase is subject to aging that leads to an increase in the electrical resistance, which is detrimental to the operation of the devices. Using a machine learning interatomic potential, we have investigated the structural relaxations responsible for aging in amorphous Ge$_2$Sb$_2$Te$_5$ in molecular dynamics simulations at temperatures slightly below the glass transition. The aging simulation, lasting about 100 ns, follows an equilibration of 24 ns at 400 K. During aging we observed an enhancement of the Peierls distortion in axial bonds which is a typical feature of these alloys that we relate to the widening of the electronic band gap computed within Density Functional Theory in smaller aged amorphous models. We also observed a marked reduction of the atomic mobility with an increase of the bond lifetimes during aging. However, we do not see a reduction in homopolar bonds, which are expected to be absent in the ideal aged glass and which should be removed on a much longer time scale.

items.title: Spin Structure Factor of the classical Ising Model on the Centered Pyrochlore Lattice
authors: L. Xu, T. Krei{\ss}el, N. Davier, L. D. C. Jaubert, L. Pollet
items.summary: We present the spin structure factor of the Ising model on the centered pyrochlore lattice. Generalizing Henley's method [Phys. Rev. B 71, 014424] to the case of inequivalent center and vertex spins, we obtain spin correlation functions that are in excellent agreement with Monte Carlo results and can capture sharp and broadened pinch points, also at finite temperature. Our approach can be extended to other centered lattice structures in classical frustrated magnetism.

items.title: Toward Self-Driving Multi-reference Calculations: Belief-Aware Orbital Selection
authors: Chen Li, Kaifan Pan, Xinyu Sun, Yinxuan Song, Lianhua He, Teng Lu, Haibo Ma, Zhenggang Lan, Yingjin Ma
items.summary: We reformulate active-orbital selection as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP), analogous to decision-making in autonomous driving and robot control, and couple it with quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) to emulate expert-like selection of active orbitals. The three popular types of orbital information, i.e. occupation numbers, orbital composition, and orbital entanglements, can be used separately or jointly. QUBO constructs complete candidate spaces under fixed electron and orbital counts, while the POMDP selects successive calculations, updates its belief from each completed result, and thereby corrects and refines the active orbitals. This belief-aware sequential procedure enables continuous active-space selection rather than one-shot threshold-based filtering, so the space can adapt as the calculation proceeds. We demonstrate the approach for valence-space construction in small molecules, spectral calculation of metal compound TiF$_3$, and active-space refinement of 1,2-dioxetanone around conical intersections. Because selection learns from calculations on the molecule of interest without requiring a pre-existing training set, it is suited to following the entire course of complex chemical reactions.

items.title: Zero-Field Optical Readout of Quintet States in Through-Space Coupled Tetracene Oligomers at Room Temperature
authors: Jeannine Gr\"une, Maciej Majdecki, William K. Myers, Przemys{\l}aw Gawe{\l}, Hannah L. Stern
items.summary: Optically addressable electron spins are promising platforms for quantum technologies, with molecular systems offering chemical control over their spin and optical properties. Achieving optical readout of molecular spin states at room temperature and without an applied magnetic field is an important step towards their practical implementation. Quintet states generated via singlet fission are promising optically addressable multilevel qudits, but their intrinsic spin transitions at zero and weak magnetic fields remain largely unexplored, while substantial room-temperature quintet coherence has predominantly been demonstrated in structurally constrained molecular architectures. Here, we combine zero-field optically detected magnetic resonance (zero-field ODMR) with transient and pulsed electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) to investigate the magnetic-field dependence and coherent spin properties of quintet states in conformationally flexible, through-space coupled tetracene oligomers. We demonstrate zero-field optical readout of quintet states at room temperature in both tetracene dimers and hexamers, and map the response of optically detected transitions to weak applied magnetic fields. Complementary EPR measurements support quintet formation through stochastic exchange fluctuations and demonstrate a room-temperature phase-memory time of 446 ns, showing that the conformational dynamics enabling high-spin formation remain compatible with substantial spin coherence. Together, these results integrate field-free optical readout, weak-field response and room-temperature spin coherence within a chemically modular, through-space coupled molecular architecture, expanding the design space for optically addressable molecular qudits and quantum sensors.

items.title: Large deviations of spatial moments of the Kipnis-Marchioro-Presutti lattice gas following a localized energy release
authors: Timo Schorlepp, Baruch Meerson, Pavel Sasorov
items.summary: We study the long-time statistics of spatial moments of the time-dependent energy distribution in a one-dimensional Kipnis-Marchioro-Presutti model following an instantaneous release of energy on a single lattice site. The moments are $M_n(T)=\sum_i x_i^n u_i(T)$, where $u_i(T)$ is the energy at site $i$ at the observation time $T$. Employing macroscopic fluctuation theory (MFT), we calculate the variance of $M_n$ for every positive integer $n$ and determine the non-Gaussian distribution tails for the representative cases $n=1$ and $2$. For the first moment, we establish an exact duality, within MFT, to integrated-current statistics for a deterministic flat initial density. For both $n=1$ and $n=2$, the large-moment tails are dominated by a single adiabatically evolving doublon: a rapidly propagating pair of narrow solitary pulses of the energy density and of the gradient of the conjugate field. The small-second-moment tail is associated with concentration of the energy near the origin at time $T$. Comparing single- and two-doublon histories, we predict a dynamical phase transition at a critical value of $M_2$ at which the optimal path breaks reflection symmetry $x\to -x$. Numerical solutions obtained by direct minimization of the MFT action establish the second-order character of this transition and support our analytical predictions. Finally, we extend calculations of the large- and small-moment tails to arbitrary $n$ and numerically find a transition of the same type for $n=4$.

items.title: Chiral-phonon-induced anomalous Hall effect in bilayer MoSe$_2$
authors: Omer Yaniv, Swati Chaudhary, Carolina Paiva, Dominik M. Juraschek
items.summary: We demonstrate that optically driven chiral phonons induce an anomalous Hall response in a nonmagnetic, centrosymmetric material. Using first-principles calculations to parameterize an effective $\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{p}$ Hamiltonian for bilayer MoSe$_2$, we show that circular excitation of an $E_u$ phonon generates a circular dynamical Rashba spin-orbit coupling. The resulting Floquet bands carry same-sign Berry curvature at the two valleys, producing a Hall response whose sign follows the phonon handedness. We obtain a range of $\sigma_{xy}\sim10^{-2}-0.21$ $\frac{e^2}{2\pi\hbar}$ for experimentally accessible light pulses. Our results show that chiral phonons provide a route to controlling electronic Berry curvature and transport on ultrafast time scales.

items.title: A Hierarchical Harmonic-to-Anharmonic Framework for ab initio Screening and Mechanistic Analysis of Negative Thermal Expansion in ZrV2O7
authors: J. Bustamante, A. Miliute, N. Jaykhedkar, A. A. Naik, J. Grandel, F. Emmerling, T. M. Stawski, J. George
items.summary: Negative thermal expansion (NTE) in framework materials arises from complex lattice dynamics that are challenging to capture using conventional theoretical approaches. Here, we establish a hierarchical computational strategy for investigating NTE in ZrV2O7, integrating the quasiharmonic approximation (QHA), temperature-dependent effective potentials (TDEP), and machine-learning-accelerated ab initio molecular dynamics (ML-MD). Quasi-harmonic lattice-dynamical calculations identify low-frequency phonon modes with negative Gr\"uneisen parameters as inexpensive screening descriptors, while TDEP incorporates finite-temperature anharmonicity and ML-MD further reveals temperature-dependent structural distortions that drive the lattice contraction. The observations are further corroborated with X-ray diffraction (XRD) measurements. The concurrent increase in transverse displacement (uT) provides microscopic evidence for a quasi-rigid-unit-mode (QRUM) mechanism underlying the NTE behaviour at elevated temperatures. This is consistent with previous reports on other framework materials, including ZrW2O7, where collective polyhedral rotations and transverse atomic motions have been linked to NTE. Overall, our results demonstrate how relatively inexpensive lattice-dynamical descriptors can identify potential NTE materials, while higher-level anharmonic simulations can then resolve the underlying structural mechanisms at the atomic scale.

items.title: Fast Accurate Quantum Monte Carlo without Metropolis Adjustment
authors: Reuben Cohn-Gordon, Gabriel Pescia, Sumner N. Hearth, Jakob Robnik, Uro\v{s} Seljak, Peter Lunts
items.summary: In quantum systems, physical quantities of interest can be expressed as expectation values of a probability distribution, which allows their estimation by Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods. This approach, an instance of Quantum Monte Carlo (QMC), plays a central role in obtaining predictions of system properties relevant to condensed matter and high energy physics. The use of Hamiltonian dynamics to design a Markov kernel, known as Hybrid or Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC), is widespread in quantum applications. In this context, it is standard to use an HMC kernel that is ``adjusted'' with the Metropolis-Hastings (MH) criterion, so that estimates of expectations converge to their true value in the limit of infinite sample size. However, recent work in computational statistics suggests that an \emph{unadjusted} HMC kernel can be significantly more efficient, while safely maintaining an asymptotic bias which is small relative to the error arising from the variance of the finite sample size. We adapt this approach to the QMC setting, focusing on a challenging and high-dimensional \emph{spin-fermion} model of a quantum phase transition. We find that unadjusted methods outperform adjusted HMC in terms of effective sample size per gradient call, while retaining accurate results.

items.title: Universal Critical Relations and Nonuniversal Scaling in Inverse-Square Ising Chains
items.summary: For ferromagnetic Ising chains with $n^2J_n\to B>0$, the critical excess magnetization in a field inversely proportional to spin separation determines the connected correlation. Their slowly varying profile has finite logarithmic integral exactly when the ordered thermal slope is finite. For any finite nonnegative core, an exact tail gives inverse-logarithmic correlations and a square-root cusp. A relative correction $c/\log(n+e)$ with $c>1$ gives continuously varying logarithmic powers and a linear cusp. A lower bound on its disordered susceptibility excludes the usual Kosterlitz--Thouless law.

items.title: Hands-on fabrication of 2D material field-effect transistors for the classroom using off-the-shelf ionic gel
authors: Yigit Sozen, Tayfun Kutlu, Juan J. Riquelme, Andres Castellanos-Gomez
items.summary: We introduce a hands-on experimental method that enables students to fabricate and operate van der Waals semiconductor-based field-effect transistors (FETs) using readily available materials and minimal infrastructure. The approach is based on ionic-gel gating using commercially available hydrogel conductors originally developed for muscle electrostimulation devices. For device fabrication we rely on commercially available thin-film interdigitated electrode arrays and for the semiconductor channel, we deposited MoS2 flakes produced by high-throughput mechanical exfoliation. By avoiding the need for cleanroom processing, vacuum deposition, or custom electrolytes, this method allows functional FETs based on van der Waals materials to be realized in a standard teaching laboratory. The experiment is well suited for undergraduate and early graduate courses and is intended to complement concepts introduced in electronics and solid-state physics by providing students with first-hand experience in the fabrication and electrical characterization of emerging electronic devices. Representative electrical measurements demonstrate gate-dependent modulation of the channel conductance and illustrate characteristic features of ionic-gated transistor operation. Overall, the proposed platform provides an accessible route for students to fabricate, characterize, and analyze field-effect devices without access to conventional semiconductor foundry.

items.title: Rotor-driven piecewise cross polarization of wide quadrupolar lines: bath-contact pumping of vector and tensor order in dynamically polarized solids
items.summary: In a dynamically polarized solid with a common nuclear spin temperature, spin-1 $^{14}$N in ammonia sits at $P_N\simeq0.14$ when the protons are at $0.90$, and a deuteron in a proton-rich matrix at $P_D\simeq0.29$. Hartmann--Hahn cross polarization (CP) from the protons could raise either toward $P_H$, but the first-order quadrupole interaction spreads the $^{14}$N line over $5$~MHz at $5$~T, far beyond any single contact bandwidth. We develop the theory of CP into one transition of a quadrupolar spin-1, with slow sample rotation carrying each crystallite through a fixed-frequency contact window. A bath contact is an idempotent map on the populations of the contacted transition, so repeated or continuous contacts accumulate rather than cancel, and the hit-once and parity constraints that force stepped rotation for pulsed inversions do not arise. In the small-reservoir limit the population ratio across the contacted transition becomes $(1+P_H)/(1-P_H)$, giving $\Pzz=+0.88$ in one contact and $\Pzz\to-1.8$ in two from $P_H=0.9$, beyond the unitary bound $[-0.85,+0.65]$. Under continuous rotation, a window at the Pake horn reaches every bond for an axis perpendicular to the field, while a window in the clean pedestal region, needed for a definite sign of tensor order, reaches a fraction $\sin2\theta_c=0.943$ at the magic angle $54.74\degree$. Steady-state order is set by the contact rate against rotation-driven cross-branch relaxation, negligible for $^{14}$N. In the cubic limit one contact places the spin-1 at the proton temperature ($\Pzz=+0.85$), but only a resolved quadrupole splitting permits negative tensor order. The limiting resource is the proton spin lock, which must far exceed the $\simeq28$~kHz local field for a contact short compared with $T_{1\rho}$, unmeasured at $1$~K. Protocols are given for $^{14}$N in NH$_3$ and deuterons in NH$_2$D.

items.title: The bias interval of the elephant random walk
items.summary: Gu\'erin, Laulin, Raschel, and Simon conjectured that the initial biases giving the superdiffusive elephant random walk a bimodal limit law form an interval centered at one half, and they described the problem as challenging. We prove this. For every superdiffusive memory, strongly biased starts are unimodal, and the limit density has two local maxima exactly when the bias lies in a proper open interval. Outside it, including its endpoints, the density has a unique local maximum. The interval is nonempty exactly above a single memory threshold, numerically about $0.6688$, whose uniqueness follows from a positive-weight integral for the central curvature of the fair-start density. We control sign changes in the finite walk's first and second differences, including those created at the boundary, and pass them to the limit. The bias boundary is continuous and tends to zero at least quadratically fast as memory tends to one.

items.title: Probing Krylov Dynamics in Driven Many-Body Systems
items.summary: Krylov complexity has become a central probe of operator growth, scrambling, and quantum chaos. Yet, a basic fact hinders its experimental study: laboratory quantum systems are routinely driven in time, whereas the Krylov construction assumes a fixed generator and breaks down once the Hamiltonian varies. Here, we solve the time-dependent many-body Krylov problem exactly and in closed form for scale- and rotation-invariant systems realized in current quantum-simulation and control platforms. We find exact relations that map the driven dynamics onto mutually orthogonal Krylov subspaces and yield a closed-form spread complexity, determined solely by the spectral properties of the initial Hamiltonian and the driving schedule. The construction extends to Liouville space and solves the time-dependent density-matrix Krylov problem, which makes the Krylov dynamics of initial thermal states experimentally accessible. In scale-invariant quantum gases, such as the driven Lieb-Liniger model, the Tonks-Girardeau gas, and the Calogero-Sutherland model, the complexity is set by the width of the atomic cloud and its rate of change, directly accessible via in situ and time-of-flight imaging. In rotation-invariant spin systems such as the Haldane-Shastry and central-spin models, it is governed by collective spin precession that can be probed and read out in trapped-ion, cavity-QED, and circuit-QED platforms.

items.title: Squeezed Light Generation by Cooper Pair Recombination in a Superconductor-Semiconductor Structure
authors: Sima Buchbinder, Avi Koriat, Alex Hayat
items.summary: We theoretically demonstrate squeezed light generation in a compact, electrically driven device utilizing the nonlinear light-matter interaction of Cooper-pair recombination in a hybrid superconductorsemiconductor structure. On the basis of second-order perturbation theory, we developed an effective Hamiltonian which incorporates the electronic component of the interaction as a photon coupling strength coefficient, enabling a model to describe the quadrature squeezing effect of Cooper-pair recombination on the photonic state. We find the squeezing strength to be proportional to the superconducting energy gap squared and device length, as well as increasing with applied voltage. For practical device length, materials and voltage bias, we calculated squeezing values comparable to those of existing squeezed light generation methods when operating below the critical temperature. This theoretically developed concept shows viability for electrically pumped squeezed light generation and can pave the way towards realization of squeezing in compact integrated structures.

items.title: Quantum synchronization in XX chains under relaxation
authors: K\"ubra S\"umer, Ege Yi\u{g}it Ald{\i}rmaz, Steve Campbell, Bar{\i}\c{s} \c{C}akmak, G\"oktu\u{g} Karpat
items.summary: We study stable synchronization in qubit XX chains with site-dependent frequencies and exchange couplings under multi-local amplitude damping noise, extending the uniform-chain results of B. \c{C}akmak et al., [Phys. Rev. A 114, L030202 2026] in several directions. We establish that the dark-mode energies are precisely the eigenvalues shared by all undamped segments separated by the damped sites. Generic stable synchronization of the edge qubits occurs if and only if these segments share exactly one eigenvalue and this eigenvalue is nonzero, in which case every qubit on the support of the corresponding dark mode is synchronized with locking constants independent of the initial preparation. This spectral matching condition identifies the Hamiltonian parameters that support synchronization, while the couplings to the damped sites control the relative oscillation amplitudes. We present analytical examples which show how inhomogeneity can create synchronization absent in uniform chains and turn preparation-dependent locking into generic synchronization. We also calculate the asymptotic pairwise concurrence and prove that, in the single-dark-mode regime, every pair participating in synchronized oscillations remains entangled with a nonzero, constant concurrence.

items.title: Emergent Anyons in a Weakly Interacting Gauged Chern Insulator
authors: Sven Bachmann, Leonardo Goller, Marcello Porta
items.summary: We derive a microscopic relation between the many-body Chern number $C$ of the fermionic ground state and the braiding of fluxes in $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ gauge theory coupled to matter: under a spectral gap condition, dressed flux loops obey $W_2W_1=e^{i\frac{\pi}{2}C}W_1W_2$ on the ground-state sector. We realize $C=1$ by gauging charge parity in a weakly interacting Qi-Wu-Zhang insulator. Reflection positivity and chessboard estimates show that flux defects are massive, which yields a gapped, topologically ordered phase with four locally indistinguishable ground states.

items.title: SunLightBots: Turning sunlight into self-sustained, high-power motion in soft robots
authors: Yoo Jin Lee, Melanie Torres Crespo, Zhongxiao Deng, Andrew Tejada-Vega, Rebecca Kramer-Bottiglio, Wenzhong Yan, Yimin Luo
items.summary: Soft robots built from active materials can directly convert environmental stimuli into motion, offering a route to energy autonomy and embodied control. However, environmental energy is generally harvested at low power, whereas rapid, mechanically demanding actions require high mechanical output power. Reconciling this mismatch while sustaining self-regulated cyclic actuation is challenging, particularly at the subgram scale, where limited payload capacity constrains the integration of conventional power and control hardware. Here, we present SunLightBots, a class of subgram, sunlight-powered, untethered soft robots that achieve autonomous locomotion under continuous illumination near 1 Sun (100 mW/cm2). Their operation is enabled by a self-resetting snapping (SRS) mechanism that integrates liquid crystal elastomers (LCEs) with snap-through instability to accumulate solar energy supplied at low power, release it as rapid, high-power motion, and reset through photothermal-mechanical feedback. Through coordinated optimization of the LCE actuation temperature, photothermal conversion, actuation stress, and structural energy barrier, the system operates near 1 Sun and achieves a peak mass-specific mechanical power of 89 W/kg. At this irradiance, the optimized LCE generates an actuation stress of 0.1 MPa at approximately 60 deg C. SunLightBots demonstrate sustained swimming, crawling, and repeated impulsive jumping. Under 1.5 Suns, the swimmer advances more than three body lengths per cycle. This work provides a materials-mechanics route toward autonomous soft robots powered entirely by the environment.

items.title: Correlation-Consistent Gaussian Basis Sets for Periodic Solids. I. Hydrogen and p-block Elements from Boron to Chlorine
items.summary: We present the cc-pVXZ-s series (X = D, T, and Q) of correlation-consistent Gaussian basis sets for solids, covering hydrogen and the p-block elements from boron to chlorine. The series includes basis sets of consistent quality for the all-electron potential and for various pseudopotentials and effective core potentials commonly used in periodic calculations. Our design combines Dunning's construction of the molecular cc-pVXZ series with a revised material-constrained atomic optimization (MCAO) algorithm for improved numerical performance. MCAO regularizes standard atomic optimization to suppress overly diffuse basis functions and ensure numerical stability in a set of reference solids. Benchmarks against standard cc-pVXZ calculations for molecules and plane-wave calculations for periodic solids establish the accuracy, transferability, and numerical stability of cc-pVXZ-s in both mean-field and correlated wavefunction calculations and confirm reliable extrapolation to the complete-basis-set (CBS) limit. As an application, we use all-electron cc-pVXZ-s to compute basis-set-converged lattice constants, bulk moduli, and cohesive energies for 7 bulk semiconductors. Using a hierarchy of correlated wavefunction methods up to local coupled cluster with singles, doubles, and perturbative triples [CCSD(T)], we find systematic convergence toward experimental bulk moduli and cohesive energies, while a small systematic overestimation of lattice constants suggests potential limitations in the approximate finite-size treatment. This work provides a foundation for the further development of systematically convergent Gaussian basis sets for periodic calculations.

items.title: Bayesian inference with a polymer probabilistic computer
authors: Travis Wanless, Yuriy Bandera, Lubomir Kostal, Stephen H. Foulger
items.summary: Bayesian inference weighs competing explanations of noisy data by sampling from a posterior distribution, a task that deterministic hardware performs only by simulating randomness. Probabilistic bits (p-bits) supply this randomness physically, but the few hardware networks of p-bits built so far use inorganic devices, address optimization or learning, and are judged without reference to the spread expected from finite sampling. Here we report a probabilistic computer built from solution-processed conjugated-polymer memristors. Four polymer p-bits, tracked online for drift and coupled in a closed Gibbs-sampling loop, sample competing, degenerate and cooperative posteriors over sixteen states with statistics that fall within the range of ideal p-bits, both in their distribution and in their autocorrelation, without any parameter fitted to the target. This agreement extends to new simulated sensor readings whose outcome was predicted before each run, including readings that point away from the true answer. Reprogrammed in software, the same circuit and controller reproduces the invertible AND gate of earlier p-bit networks, with its temperature fixed in advance rather than fitted. Polymer p-bits thus open a route to printed, large-area probabilistic computers that infer alongside their sensors.

items.title: Randomly growing uniform hypergraphs
items.summary: We investigate growing uniform random hypergraphs whose hyperedges are $(k-1)$-simplices. At each step, one of two processes occurs: (i) a new vertex is added with probability $p$; (ii) a simplex $\langle v_1,\ldots,v_k\rangle$ with randomly chosen distinct vertices is added with probability $1-p$. Emerging random uniform hypergraphs exhibit a percolation transition. A giant component is formed when $p<p_c=1-(2k-1)^{-2}$. The fraction of vertices in the giant component scales as $\exp[-C/\sqrt{p_c-p}]$, a signature of the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless phase transition. In the non-percolating phase, the cluster size distribution has an algebraic tail with a continuously varying exponent, while at $p=p_c$, it acquires a logarithmic correction. We analyze triadic hypergraphs ($k=3$) in detail and then generalize to higher $k$. We show that the Euler characteristic and the first Betti number of the giant component scale linearly with system size. Higher Betti numbers fluctuate between realizations but remain finite, and hence the normalized Euler characteristic and the first Betti number of the giant component are asymptotically equal, up to a sign.

items.title: Spontaneous mechanical patterning in active elastic tissues with stress feedback
authors: Henrik Weyer, Divyoj Singh, M. Cristina Marchetti
items.summary: The active mechanics of biological tissues is often governed by embedded active contractile fibers responding to mechanical feedback. We introduce a minimal model of a solid-like tissue where the mechanics is controlled by feedback of local active and elastic stresses on fiber organization. The resulting tissue generically exhibits a bistable response to external strain and spontaneously segregates into domains of orthogonally aligned fibers. Our theory thus provides a minimal mechanical feedback mechanism generating orthogonal structural alignment ubiquitous in biological tissues.

items.title: Distilling an atomistic foundation model is all you need for large-scale molecular dynamics of semiconductor interfaces
authors: Feiyu Zhou, Wei Qiu, Fei Shuang, Yilun Liu, Shengying Yue, Penghua Ying
items.summary: State-of-the-art atomistic foundation models provide broadly transferable energy and force predictions, but their direct deployment in large-scale molecular dynamics remains computationally costly. Here we examine whether their knowledge can be distilled into compact potentials while retaining the physical responses of heterogeneous semiconductor interfaces. From 128 pretrained models spanning 22 model families, we select a fixed EquiformerV3 teacher and train atomic cluster expansion (ACE) and neuroevolution potential (NEP) students without target-specific teacher fine-tuning, with both simulation speed and accessible system size improved by several orders of magnitude relative to the teacher model. Matched training configurations and architectures enable direct comparisons with students trained on density-functional-theory (DFT) reference labels. For 79,920-atom BAs/GaN interfaces, direct distillation preserves termination-dependent thermal conductance and dominant spectral features, with conductance differing by at most 6.6% from DFT-trained counterparts. In 29,792-atom Cu/diamond specimens loaded at 500 K, tensile strength and loading work differ by 2.8% and 1.5%, respectively. Exploratory SiC/a-C/SiC simulations retain the principal thermal bottleneck and the direction of the annealing response. Furthermore, a four-model committee retrieves 42-56% of the highest-error teacher configurations with a 10% selection budget and improves high-error force fitting, but does not consistently improve downstream properties. These findings demonstrate that direct distillation can preserve key interfacial thermal and mechanical responses in compact interatomic potentials, opening a path towards large-scale, high-throughput simulations of heterogeneous interfaces.

items.title: Feedback-induced mechanical bistability and perpendicular-domain formation in active elastic tissues
authors: Divyoj Singh, Henrik Weyer, Harry Kroft, M. Cristina Marchetti
items.summary: Contractile fibers in muscle tissues are highly aligned over the scale of many cells. Muscle layers surrounding organs with an inner lumen are often arranged in orthogonal directions. Here, we study a minimal mechanism of how structural order and its patterning into orthogonally aligned domains can emerge from mechanical feedback alone. The central idea is that contractile fibers align in the direction of the local active and elastic stresses, a feedback motivated by the maturation of muscle fibers under tension. We thus model muscle tissue as an active nematic solid with stress feedback: an elastic medium with embedded contractile fibers that are reinforced along the directions of the local tissue stresses. We find that the feedback from the contractile fiber stress is self-amplifying and drives spontaneous fiber alignment. Feedback from the elastic stress couples the alignment to the mechanical boundary conditions and tissue geometry. Depending on the mechanical boundary conditions, the elastic-stress feedback stabilizes two orthogonally aligned tissue states, resulting in a structurally and mechanically bistable tissue that shows a hysteretic stress-strain response. In spatially extended tissues, this bistability gives rise to orthogonally aligned domains separated by domain walls. In an annulus surrounding a pressurized lumen, a radially aligned inner domain and a circumferentially aligned outer domain stably coexist because the domain wall is pinned at a position that results in the fibers carrying the lumen pressure. Our results show that stress feedback can pattern structural order by coupling spontaneous alignment to the tissue geometry. Our mechanism thus provides a purely mechanical route to orthogonal fiber patterning in muscle tissues.

items.title: Local enhancement of finite-strength code preparation: recoverability and Wilson coherence
authors: Tong Xu, Yuanchen Zhao, Dong E. Liu
items.summary: Stabilizer measurements provide a direct route to preparing quantum error-correcting codes and long-range entangled states. In realistic implementations, however, finite measurement strength can coherently deform the encoding map away from the projective limit. Certain nonlocal signatures associated with long-range order can survive such a deformation, but this alone does not guarantee that the resulting state protects encoded quantum information. We show that, at fixed strength, local logical leakage obstructs asymptotically faithful recovery; along logical operators' supports, its accumulation forces the relevant measurement strength to grow logarithmically with code distance. We then prove that this obstruction can be removed locally: for fixed toric registers under sufficiently weak local-stochastic errors, enhancing only a vanishing fraction of checks near selected logical supports restores recovery while the bulk remains at finite measurement strength. With recoverability restored, we prove a further dimensional distinction in logical operations. In the strict three-dimensional deconfined phase, suitable enhanced tubes restore the equivalence of macroscopically separated representatives, so either representative asymptotically implements the same controlled logical action on a fixed encoding. In two dimensions, recoverability alone does not restore this equivalence: the representatives can remain inequivalent even when both associated encodings are recoverable.

items.title: A unified finite-site framework for scaffold-client biocondensation
items.summary: Client recruitment into biomolecular condensates does not determine how stronger binding changes the bulk free-energy advantage of demixing. Here, we use a unified finite-site thermodynamic framework to examine how scaffold-client interactions affect both the response of a fixed-composition mixture and the organization of its ternary phase diagram. The thermodynamic response to increasing client affinity is determined by the difference in heterotypic bonding between the complete equilibrium phase-separated sample and the corresponding homogeneous state. A finite region of the model exhibits positive scaffold-client concentration covariance but negative heterotypic bond contrast: stronger binding reduces the demixing advantage even when both species enrich in the dense phase. This reduction also occurs with independent scaffold self-association and client-binding site pools, without direct displacement of scaffold bonds. A negative response does not by itself imply condensate shrinkage or dissolution. Across composition space, the same finite binding constraints support scaffold-rich and heterotypic coexistence regimes with distinct bond populations. For divalent clients, these regimes can occupy disconnected regions of the phase diagram and reconnect upon increasing client affinity, depending on scaffold cohesion. Critical-point continuation identifies the folds and cusp organizing these changes, while client valence restricts the parameter range over which disconnected coexistence occurs. Explicit-particle Monte Carlo simulations reproduce the qualitative reentrant response and provide finite-size evidence for disconnected coexistence. These results provide a bond-resolved characterization of fixed-parent affinity response and a complementary description of coexistence under specified association constraints.

items.title: Reducing TLS Losses in Superconducting Circuits Using Solid Neon
authors: A. Palmer, K. Matkovic, P. Russell, E. Helgemo, L. Delventhal, Y. Ashlea Alava, K. Zuo, S. N. Coppersmith, M. C. Cassidy
items.summary: Two level systems (TLSs) are a major source of loss in superconducting devices, limiting the performance of qubits, detectors, and resonators. These defects arise from a range of sources, including surface oxides, crystal defects, as well as fabrication residues which are often difficult to remove. Using NbTiN coplanar waveguide resonators, we show that depositing and subsequently removing a solid neon film can significantly improve device performance. Analysis of the temperature and power dependence indicates that this enhancement arises from reduced TLS dissipation, which we attribute to the redistribution and removal of surface contaminants during neon deposition and evaporation. Atomic force microscopy images of contaminated hexagonal boron nitride flakes before and after neon exposure show that neon treatment can redistribute and remove surface residues. These results demonstrate a simple, non-destructive approach for mitigating TLS losses in superconducting devices and other sensitive materials that cannot withstand aggressive cleaning processes.

items.title: Crystal Nucleation Driven by Microjets from Hydrodynamically Interacting Thermocavitation Bubbles
authors: Nagaraj Nagalingam, Adithya Vignesh, Vikram Korede, Herman J. M. Kramer, Peter J. T. Verheijen, Jan Groenewold, Remco Hartkamp, Johan T. Padding, Huseyin Burak Eral
items.summary: Primary nucleation predominantly dictates the physicochemical, optical and mechanical properties of crystals emerging from solution. Here, we reveal a previously unrecognized nucleation mechanism arising from bubble-bubble hydrodynamic interactions using laser-induced thermocavitation bubble pairs. Under confinement, antiphase generation of two bubbles produces a micron-scale, high-speed liquid jet. Upon impact with the surrounding supersaturated liquid, this microjet generates intense localized shear, thereby inducing crystallization of the model inorganic salt, potassium permanganate. Under identical laser energies and supersaturation levels, crystallization was not observed in single-bubble experiments, in which no microjet was present. We show that the crystallization probability increases with microjet velocity. Boundary integral simulations reveal how experimental parameters such as confinement, bubble spacing, and laser energy govern microjet formation and velocity. We quantify the relationship between jet velocity and the observed enhancement in crystal nucleation kinetics by incorporating shear into the kinetic prefactor in classical nucleation theory. By combining experiments, theory, and simulations, we establish how microjets emerging from bubble-bubble hydrodynamic interactions may influence crystallization kinetics, opening new opportunities for the manufacture of crystalline materials.

items.title: Cumulants of Operator Semigroups for Hierarchies of Many-Particle Evolution Equations
items.summary: The paper presents a brief overview of recent advances in the mathematical theory of evolution equations for quantum many-particle systems. The structure of expansions representing non-perturbative solutions to the Cauchy problem for hierarchies of fundamental evolution equations for many quantum particles is outlined. It has been shown that the concept of cumulants of operator semigroups forms the basis for non-perturbative representation of solutions to hierarchies of evolution equations that describe the state and observables. It is proven that the constructed dynamics of correlations underlie the description of the evolution of the state, both for finitely and infinitely many particles, governed by the BBGKY hierarchy for reduced density operators or by the hierarchy of nonlinear evolution equations for reduced correlation operators. In fact, it is demonstrated that the behavior of particle correlations governs the dynamics of states in quantum systems with an infinite number of particles.

items.title: Quantization Breaks Classical Mpemba Constraints
authors: Yue Liu, Tan Van Vu, Fr\'ed\'eric van Wijland, Hisao Hayakawa
items.summary: The Mpemba effect, in which an initially hotter system relaxes faster than a colder one, has been widely studied in both classical and quantum systems, yet identifying the specific effects of quantization requires a consistent comparison with the corresponding classical dynamics. Starting from the Caldeira-Leggett model, we establish a quantum-classical correspondence for thermal relaxation. We find that the locality of classical energy diffusion forbids the Mpemba effect in single-well and symmetric double-well potentials. Conversely, quantum dynamics allows for direct transitions between nonadjacent energy levels, overcoming the constraints of classical local energy diffusion and enabling the Mpemba effect in these potentials. In the semiclassical limit $\hbar\to0$, the nonlocal transitions become increasingly suppressed, restoring the classical constraints. Our findings reveal that quantization fundamentally unlocks anomalous relaxation pathways, rather than merely modifying relaxation rates.

items.title: Are Scaling Laws of Universal MLIPs Universal?
authors: Theo Keane, Anthony Onwuli, Richard Tomsett, Robert M. Forrest, Jonathan J. Bean
items.summary: Neural scaling laws enable the prediction of returns from larger training datasets, but machine-learned interatomic potential (MLIP) datasets are heterogeneous and expensive to generate, and equal numbers of structures need not contain equal amounts of useful information. We study data scaling under fixed model configurations for M3GNet, MACE, and PET trained on subsets of a combined MatPES-MP-ALOE training pool. Across training structure subsets from 10,000 to 640,000, together with the full 1.16-million-structure training set, we compare uniform random sampling, three chemistry- and structure-informed stratification policies, iterative DIRECT, and furthest-point sampling using embeddings from three pretrained MLIPs. Models are evaluated using cohesive-energy, force, stress, and aggregate losses on both a held-out test set from the parent distribution and the distribution shifted MP-r$^2$SCAN test set. We observe power-law scaling improvements with increasing data, but the fitted scaling exponent, apparent error floor, and relative sample efficiency depend on the model architecture, target quantity, data sampling policy, and test set distribution. Sampling-policy rankings can reverse across test distributions: chemical stratification can improve cross-dataset performance while degrading in-distribution performance, whereas the embedding-space diversity policies frequently under-perform random sampling. Relative loss is strongly associated with test-to-train chemical-space divergence. These results show that structure count is a necessary but insufficient scaling variable for MLIPs. For training MLIPs, the return on additional first-principles calculations depends not only on how many additional structures are included, but also on how their chemical and configurational content aligns with the model's intended use.

items.title: Defect-induced stabilization of Wigner negativity and parity-protected phase-locking
items.summary: We show that a parity-preserving delta-shaped potential, mimicking the presence of a localized defect, reduces the continuous $U(1)$-symmetry of a quantum van der Pol oscillator to the discrete $\mathbb{Z}_2$-symmetry. This mechanism guarantees protected even-parity stationary quantum coherences, resulting in the generation of non-classical steady-states characterized by Wigner function negativity. Thanks to a non-trivial interplay between the defect and non-linear dissipative channels, this kind of negativity entails parity-protected quantum phase locking, meaning that the oscillator's energy levels simultaneously lock into two opposite phases. Finally, we present a realistic experimental proposal involving the motional state of ultracold alkaline-earth-like atoms in optical tweezers, where the localized defect is engineered via state-selective contact interactions, while the non-linear dissipative channels are driven by Raman sidebands.

items.title: A general formula for the amplitude-frequency ratio in shaking induced Mott insulator of atomtronic transistors
authors: Wenxi Lai, Yu-Quan Ma, Yi-Wen Wei
items.summary: Mott insulator of atomic transport can be realized in shaken optical lattices by choosing particular ratio of driving amplitude and frequency, which has been studied as Floquet engineering with time-independent effective Hamiltonian approach. Here, we give a general formula of amplitude-frequency ratio for realization of the shaking induced insulator-conductor transition in a double-well open system, using numerical computation with instantaneous eigenstates approach. The result is owing to the fact that the instantaneous eigenstates approach is applicable in wider parameter range compared with the time-independent effective Hamiltonian approach. Analysis from the results of quantum master equation shows that the insulator effect is originated from coherent localization of atom wave packets in optical wells.

items.title: An Infinite Two-Parameter Family of Octagonal Tilings
authors: April Lynne D. Say-awen, Sam Coates
items.summary: We construct an infinite two-parameter family of substitution rules with inflation factors $\delta_{(m,n)}=m+n(1+\sqrt{2})$ for integers $m\geq0$ and $n\geq1$, excluding pairs in which $m$ is even and $n$ is odd. Extending four examples from our previous work, we show that each substitution admits a tiling with $8$-fold rotational symmetry and that the associated tilings are repetitive and have finite local complexity. We also classify the inflation factors according to their PV and unimodular properties and illustrate selected cases through perpendicular-space projections and Fourier spectra.

items.title: Quantum geometric ferromagnetism by singular saddle point
authors: Taisei Kitamura, Hiroki Nakai, Akito Daido, Youichi Yanase
items.summary: We propose ferromagnetism that occurs in electrons at a saddle point with band touching, which we call the singular saddle point. At the singular saddle point, the divergent quantum metric induces ferromagnetic correlation, and the logarithmic divergence of the density of states ensures ferromagnetism within Stoner theory. This is a prototypical example of quantum geometric ferromagnetism. The two-dimensional $t_{2g}$-orbital model accommodates the ferromagnetism by this mechanism, which is continuously connected to the exactly proven flat-band ferromagnetism.

items.title: Continuous symmetry breaking in 1D spin chains and 1+1D field theory
items.summary: We argue that ground states of 1D spin chains can spontaneously break U(1) ``easy-plane'' spin rotation symmetry, via true long-range order of $(S^x, S^y)$, at the phase transition between two quasi-long-range-ordered phases. The critical point can be reached by tuning a single parameter in a Hamiltonian with the same symmetry as the XXZ model, without further fine-tuning. Equivalently, it can arise in systems of bosons with particle-hole symmetry, as a long-range-ordered transition point between two quasi-long-range-ordered superfluids. Our approach is to start with the continuum field theory of the isotropic Heisenberg ferromagnet and consider generic perturbations that respect easy-plane symmetry. We argue for a renormalization-group flow to a critical point where long-range order in $(S^x, S^y)$ is enabled by coexisting critical fluctuations of $S^z$. (We also discuss multicritical points where further parameters are tuned to zero.) These results show that it is much easier to break continuous symmetries in 1D than standard lore would suggest. The failure of standard intuition for 1D chains (based on the quantum--classical correspondence) can be attributed to Berry phases, which prevent the 1+1D system from mapping to a classical 2D spin model. The present theory also gives an example of an ordered state whose Goldstone mode is interacting even in the infra-red, rather than becoming a free field.

items.title: Evidence for time-reversal symmetry breaking and glassy dynamics in superconducting (La,Pr,Sm)3Ni2O7 films
authors: Haoran Ji, Zheyuan Xie, Yaqi Chen, Guangdi Zhou, Keyi Liang, Rui Liu, Mengqiao Geng, Meixuan Li, Longxin Pan, Heng Wang, Haoliang Huang, Jun Ge, Yi Liu, Yang Liu, Guang-Ming Zhang, Yihua Wang, Ziqiang Wang, Qi-Kun Xue, Zhuoyu Chen, Jian Wang
items.summary: Superconductivity and magnetism are generally distinct and competing orders, characterized by different broken symmetries and order parameters. Although they may coexist in some correlated systems, whether and how these orders can become inherently intertwined in unconventional high-transition-temperature (high-Tc) superconductors remains a central open question. Here, we report time-reversal symmetry (TRS) breaking and glassy dynamics in the superconducting state of nickelate (La,Pr,Sm)3Ni2O7 films. Magnetoresistance hysteresis and zero-field non-reciprocal charge transport, complementary evidence for broken TRS, are observed in the superconducting state, while absent in the normal state. Within the superconducting transition regime, logarithmically slow resistance relaxations following magnetic-field perturbations provide strong evidence for glassy dynamics. Remarkably, the reproducible temperature hierarchy across multiple films reveals that these novel phenomena emerge concurrently with developing superconducting phase coherence, preceding the zero-resistance state. Consistently, scanning superconducting quantum interference device (sSQUID) microscopy directly resolves the zero-field magnetic-flux patterns indicative of spontaneous TRS breaking, which emerge simultaneously with local superconducting diamagnetism and phase stiffness. Our observations suggest a frustrated multicomponent superconducting order parameter in the nickelate films, whose internal relative phases may carry TRS-breaking chirality and freeze into a textured phase glass. Collectively, our findings identify a distinctive form of superconductivity in which internal phase degrees of freedom may support additional broken symmetries and glassy order, offering a new perspective on intertwined ordering phenomena in unconventional high-Tc superconductors.

items.title: Multiple Many-Body Localization Transitions in Driven Non-Hermitian Chains with Spatially Correlated Potentials
authors: Sanchayan Banerjee, Ayan Banerjee, Tapan Mishra, Flore K. Kunst
items.summary: We investigate the fate of a many-body-localized phase in a periodically driven non-Hermitian chain of hard-core bosons with directed hopping subject to a binary onsite potential in the form of a deterministic quasiperiodic Fibonacci sequence. While Floquet heating generally results in the thermalization of the many-body-localized system with increasing driving period, our initially many-body-localized phase displays a sequence of localization-delocalization transitions, leaving isolated extended islands between many-body-localized phases. Non-Hermiticity makes these extended islands strongly boundary sensitive, and gives rise to a Floquet many-body skin effect under open boundary conditions. We show that the re-entrant many-body localization~(MBL) is independent of our choice of potential by reproducing this phenomenology when instead considering a potential with a genuinely disordered random-dimer sequence. Furthermore, we find that the directed hopping plays a dual role: it stabilizes MBL in regimes that are only weakly localized in the Hermitian limit, while promoting delocalization and broadening extended regions elsewhere. Our work advances the fundamental understanding of non-Hermitian and nonequilibrium quantum matter by revealing how directed hopping and spatial correlations in the onsite landscape jointly govern MBL in periodically driven interacting systems

items.title: Magnetocaloric effect for the altermagnetic candidate MnTe
authors: N. N. Orlova, V. D. Esin, A. V. Timonina, N. N. Kolesnikov, E. V. Deviatov
items.summary: We experimentally investigate magnetocaloric effect for single crystals of altermagnetic candidate MnTe at the transition to the state with spontaneous spin polarization, i.e. well below the N\'eel temperature of MnTe. The isothermal magnetic entropy change $\Delta S$ is calculated from the experimental magnetization curves by using Maxwell relation. We observe well-defined magnetocaloric effect as a narrow $\Delta S$ peak around the critical temperature $T_c\approx 81$~K, which reflects the sharp magnetization jump. This behavior is unusual for standard ferromagnetic transitions, so it confirms the predicted spin-orbit-induced spin polarization in the MnTe altermagnetic state and, therefore, confirms MnTe as a prototypical altermagnet candidate.

items.title: Demon's variational principle for informational active matter
authors: Kento Yasuda, Kenta Ishimoto, Shigeyuki Komura
items.summary: The interplay between information, dissipation, and control is reshaping our understanding of thermodynamics in feedback-regulated systems. We develop the informational Onsager-Machlup principle, a generalized variational framework that unifies energetic, dissipative, and informational contributions within a single formalism. This framework introduces a conditioned Onsager-Machlup integral to quantify path entropy under specified memory states and enables the derivation of cumulant generating functions for arbitrary observables in systems with measurement and feedback. Our formulation is consistent with stochastic thermodynamics and information thermodynamics. To demonstrate the utility of the IOMP, we apply it to an information swimmer and show that it systematically reproduces the analytical expressions for the mean velocity and higher-order cumulants obtained by a direct approach, while also enabling the calculation of entropy production in the single-measurement case. For repeated measurements and the steady state, we derive approximate analytical expressions by using a Gaussian closure for the distribution of measured velocities. Our analytical results show good agreement with numerical results, except for cases of extreme drag asymmetry.

items.title: Manipulating anomalous transport via crystal symmetry in two-dimensional altermagnets
authors: Dan Li, Shuaiyu Wang, Jiabin chen, Zeling Li, Chaoxi Cui, Lei Li, Lei Wang, Zhi-Ming Yu, Xiaodong Zhou, Xiao-Ping Li
items.summary: Anomalous transports, including the anomalous Hall effect (AHE) and anomalous Nernst effect (ANE), are typical manifestations of time-reversal-symmetry-breaking responses in materials. In general, the two Hall states with opposite Hall conductivities can be regarded as time-reversal pairs coupled to magnetic order, and switching between them relies on reversing the magnetization via an external magnetic field or electric current. Here, we introduce an approach for manipulating anomalous transport through crystal symmetry engineering in two-dimensional (2D) altermagnetic systems. Through symmetry analysis and lattice models, we show that for systems with out-of-plane N\'eel vectors, breaking the symmetry that connects two magnetic sublattices will induce an anomalous Hall response. Crucially, the signs of the anomalous Hall and anomalous Nernst conductivities can be flexibly controlled via symmetry-breaking perturbations, enabling the realizing tunable sign-reversible anomalous transport. Using first-principles calculations, we investigate crystal-symmetry-controlled anomalous transport in the 2D altermagnetic materials V$_{2}$STeO and Cr$_{2}$O$_{2}$. The results indicate that these systems with out-of-plane N\'eel vectors exhibit pronounced AHE and ANE signals under uniaxial strain. Remarkably, the sign of the anomalous transport coefficients can be reversed by simply rotating the strain direction by $\pi/2$, thus enabling the switching of anomalous transverse currents without an external magnetic field. Our findings provide a new strategy to manipulate anomalous transport, and should have significant potential applications.

items.title: When does a lattice higher-form symmetry flow to a topological higher-form symmetry at low energies?
authors: Ruizhi Liu, Pok Man Tam, Ho Tat Lam, Liujun Zou
items.summary: We study the lattice version of higher-form symmetries on tensor-product Hilbert spaces. Interestingly, at low energies, these symmetries may not flow to the topological higher-form symmetries familiar from relativistic quantum field theories, but instead to non-topological higher-form symmetries. We present concrete lattice models exhibiting this phenomenon. One particular model is an $\mathbb{R}$ generalization of the Kitaev honeycomb model featuring an $\mathbb{R}$ lattice 1-form symmetry. We show that its low-energy effective field theory is a gapless, non-relativistic theory with a non-topological $\mathbb{R}$ 1-form symmetry. In both the lattice model and the effective field theory, we demonstrate that the non-topological $\mathbb{R}$ 1-form symmetry is not robust against local perturbations. In contrast, we also study various modifications of the toric code and their low-energy effective field theories to demonstrate that the compact $\mathbb{Z}_2$ lattice 1-form symmetry does become topological at low energies unless the Hamiltonian is fine-tuned. Along the way, we clarify the rules for constructing low-energy effective field theories in the presence of multiple superselection sectors. Finally, we argue on general grounds that non-compact higher-form symmetries (such as $\mathbb{R}$ and $\mathbb{Z}$ 1-form symmetries) in lattice systems generically remain non-topological at low energies, whereas compact higher-form symmetries (such as $\mathbb{Z}_{n}$ and $U(1)$ 1-form symmetries) generically become topological.

items.title: Confinement Limits Cell Shape and Mitotic Pressure During Division
items.summary: Cells often divide under mechanical confinement, where surrounding structures restrict shape changes during cytokinesis. We analyze a minimal model of a dividing cell as an incompressible volume bounded by an interface with effective isotropic tension, and show that confinement imposes a minimum attainable furrow radius. Beyond this limit, the cytokinetic ring can continue to contract within a septum without further furrow ingression, leaving the cell shape, mitotic pressure, and transmitted force unchanged. We determine this confinement-limited state for rigid parallel walls, soft axial confinement, and three-dimensional enclosures. Between parallel walls, the limiting force and minimum furrow radius collapse onto universal curves when scaled by surface tension and cell size. In soft confinement, environmental stiffness and spindle forces select the operating point. In three-dimensional confinement, the free volume between the cell and the confinement controls force transmission and cell shape. This yields a method for inferring the mechanical state of a cell dividing in deformable three-dimensional confinement from its shape. The radius and tangent angle of the cell surface at the stalled furrow and at the point where the cell detaches from its surroundings determine the mitotic pressure and the axial force carried by the cell surface, relative to the cortical tension.

items.title: peapods: A Rust-Accelerated Monte Carlo Package for Ising and XY Spin Systems
items.summary: We present peapods, an open-source Python package for Monte Carlo simulation of classical spin models with arbitrary couplings, whose sampling loop runs in Rust. It samples Ising models on periodic Bravais lattices given by user-specified neighbor offsets, optionally with open or antiperiodic boundaries, and XY models with signed couplings and site dilution on hypercubic lattices. Besides Metropolis and heat-bath sweeps, Swendsen-Wang and Wolff cluster updates and parallel tempering, it provides a family of replica cluster moves for spin glasses: the Houdayer, J\"org and Chayes-Machta-Redner moves, multi-pair variants of the first two, replica-permutation moves and a gauged form of them, and Swendsen-Wang replica Monte Carlo across temperatures. The same-temperature moves share one construction, a symmetry of the replicas' joint energy applied on clusters, and one-step stationarity tests from exact Boltzmann samples on small lattices check each family of moves that satisfies detailed balance. The package measures overlap distributions, spin-glass correlation lengths, autocorrelation times, equilibration and tempering-flow diagnostics, and jackknife errors over disorder samples. It reproduces the exact critical temperatures of the square and triangular Ising lattices, and its Binder curves for simple-cubic, BCC and FCC lattices agree at the literature critical temperatures. For the three-dimensional $\pm J$ spin glass, the crossings of $\xi_{\mathrm{SG}}/L$ for $L \le 12$ extrapolate, with the Janus correction exponent held fixed, to $T_c = 1.085(42)$, consistent with the Janus value $1.1019(29)$. For the two-dimensional XY model, the helicity modulus, correlation length and structure factor agree with high-precision reference data within $1.9$ standard errors. This article describes version 0.3.0.

items.title: Interfacial charge-transfer in 3d/5d complex oxide heterostructures
authors: Arun Kumar Jaiswal, Di Wang, Ji Soo Lim, Shruti Roy, Fabrice Wilhelm, Vanessa Wollersen, Andrei Rogalev, Matthieu Le Tacon, Dirk Fuchs
items.summary: Interfacial charge transfer (ICT) provides a powerful route to engineer electronic phases in correlated oxide heterostructures, yet predictive design principles remain elusive. Here, we systematically investigate superlattices composed of the 5d spin orbit coupled semimetal SrIrO3 and a series of correlated 3d perovskites (LaMnO3, LaFeO3, and LaCoO3), thereby establishing a quantitative framework for ICT across 3d/5d interfaces. Combining Ir L2,3 edge X ray absorption spectroscopy with spatially resolved electron energy loss spectroscopy, we estimate the electron depletion in the SrIrO3 layers and the corresponding electron accumulation in the 3d layers. The magnitude of ICT follows the trend expected from electronegativity mismatch, supporting electronegativity driven band alignment as the dominant contribution in this series. Beyond interfacial doping, we find that strong 3d,5d hybridization induces a low spin to high spin conversion in the cobaltate layers, hinting to interface controlled spin state engineering without chemical substitution. These results establish electronegativity mismatch as a predictive design parameter for correlated oxide interfaces and provide a materials platform for tailoring band filling, orbital hierarchy, and spin configurations in quantum oxide heterostructures, paving the way towards advanced oxide electronics and next-generation information technologies.

items.title: The Mpemba effect likes to hit a wall
authors: Yue Liu, Tan Van Vu, Rapha\"el Ch\'etrite, Fr\'ed\'eric van Wijland, Hisao Hayakawa
items.summary: The original Mpemba effect refers to the counterintuitive possibility that a system prepared at a higher temperature relaxes to a colder equilibrium faster than one prepared at a lower temperature. In microscopic classical realizations, this phenomenon has been studied for overdamped particles in external potentials and observed experimentally. We show that, for a particle in an asymmetric polynomial double-well potential, the one-dimensional Mpemba effect is controlled not by the double-well structure or metastability itself, but by the high-energy confinement: a hard boundary, or more generally a sufficiently steep confining tail, on the shallow side can induce the required population inversion. For the polynomial potentials considered here, the effect disappears when both hard boundaries are taken to infinity, whereas sufficiently asymmetric soft tails can play the same role as walls. We identify the underlying mechanism as a redistribution of the initial equilibrium population when it begins to probe the high-energy tails of the potential, a picture that also extends to single-well and symmetric double-well potentials.

items.title: Giant spontaneous Kerr effect and its self-doping dependence in altermagnetic MnTe
authors: Weitung Yang, Choongjae Won, Cory Cress, Weihang Lu, Xiaochen Fang, Shelby Fields, Nicholas Combs, Shaofeng Han, Marshall Zachary Franklin, Steven P. Bennett, Sang-Wook Cheong, Jing Xia
items.summary: Altermagnetism, a third class of collinear magnetism with spin-split bands and vanishing net magnetization, has emerged in hexagonal {\alpha}-MnTe, a promising platform for ultrafast, stray-field-free spintronics. Whether MnTe's macroscopic symmetry-breaking signatures reflect ideal altermagnetic order or are activated by defects remains open. Here we report giant spontaneous Kerr rotations of up to 1500 rad in {\alpha}-MnTe single crystals at the telecommunication wavelength of 1550 nm, onsetting precisely at the N\'eel temperature TN = 307 K. The signal appears in disjoint macroscopic patches whose amplitude tracks the sample conductivity, and a hole-conducting {\alpha}-MnTe film reproduces this response together with an anomalous Hall effect.
